title: Reproduction in human beings
status: draft: written 18 Nov 2026 offline for Grade 8 Integrated Science; not yet checked by a CBC Integrated Science teacher; not loaded by the live tutor
notes: Taught as the school decides, with a female and a male teacher or the guidance counsellor. Diagrams and a cycle calendar, never photographs. Health statements are to be confirmed by a teacher or a health worker; questions never ask about personal experience.

skills.key_step: The child outlines the menstrual cycle (about 28 days on average, bleeding three to seven days, ovulation near the middle), says it is normal, and names its common challenges.

floor.prerequisite: Can name the parts of the female reproductive system.
floor.question: What do the ovaries release?

representations: a labelled diagram of the uterus lining
steps: Day 1 to about day 5: the lining of the uterus is shed (menstruation).
No fertilisation: the cycle starts again. Cycles vary in length.

board.do: Draw a circle split into 28 days.
Point at the middle of the circle.

misconceptions.ask: Is that the bleeding or the whole cycle?
misconceptions.repair: The cycle is about 28 days; bleeding three to seven.

listen_for: the egg comes at the start
misconceptions.ask: Where did we mark ovulation on the circle?
Is it a normal part of growing up?
Is 28 days a rule or an average?

checks.question: About how long is the menstrual cycle on average?
About when in the cycle is an egg released?

skills.key_step: The child picks the parts of a plan that manage menstrual challenges: clean pads changed every four to six hours, daily bathing, a spare pad, rest and warm drinks for cramps, talking to a trusted adult, a health worker for severe pain, and staying in school.

floor.prerequisite: Knows the menstrual cycle is normal.
floor.question: Is menstruation an illness?

representations: a plan template: challenge, what I will do, who can help
steps: Know when to see a health worker.

board.do: Write "My period starts during a lesson".

board.say: What should be in her plan?

board.do: Wait for "a spare pad, tell the school nurse, stay in school".
Ask the child to add one more step to the plan.

misconceptions.ask: Who at school can help with a pad?
misconceptions.repair: Stay in school; carry a spare pad.

misconceptions.ask: What happens with a pad left too long?
misconceptions.repair: Change it every four to six hours.

misconceptions.ask: Which pain needs a health worker?
misconceptions.repair: Severe pain needs a health worker.

misconceptions.ask: Who is a trusted adult at school?

checks.question: How often should a pad be changed?
When should a girl see a health worker about her period?
checks.answer: if pain stops her daily life, bleeding is very heavy, or a period lasts more than a week

skills.key_step: The child describes the order: one sperm joins the egg in the oviduct (fertilisation) to make a zygote, which divides as it moves to the uterus and sinks into its lining (implantation).

floor.question: When is an egg released?
floor.answer: about the middle of the cycle

representations: a diagram of the oviduct and uterus with arrows
steps: One sperm joins it: fertilisation, a zygote.
The zygote divides as it moves down.
It sinks into the uterus lining: implantation.

board.do: Draw the oviduct leading to the uterus.
Ask the child to mark where implantation happens.

misconceptions.ask: Where does the egg meet the sperm?
Can a zygote implant before it is made?
How many cells is a zygote?
misconceptions.repair: The zygote is the first cell.

misconceptions.ask: How many sperm enter the egg?

checks.question: What is implantation?
checks.answer: the embryo sinking into the lining of the uterus

skills.key_step: The child names symptoms of common STIs (sores, unusual discharge, pain when urinating, itching), says some have no symptoms, names prevention (abstinence, faithfulness to one uninfected partner, correct condom use, testing) and says to see a health worker early.

floor.prerequisite: Knows the parts of the reproductive system.
floor.question: Where does fertilisation happen?

representations: a chart: symptom, what to do
steps: STIs spread through sexual contact (and some through blood or from mother to baby).
Symptoms, and that some have none.
See a health worker early; many can be treated.
contexts: a myth heard from a friend

misconceptions.repair: Not by hugging or toilet seats.

misconceptions.ask: Can a health worker treat many STIs?
Can washing remove an infection inside the body?
How can a person know for sure?
misconceptions.repair: Some STIs show no signs; testing shows them.

checks.question: Give one symptom of an STI.
checks.answer: sores, unusual discharge, pain when urinating or itching

checks.question: Give one way to prevent STIs.
checks.answer: abstinence, or faithfulness to one uninfected partner
